scope.current_boundary: Establish rotational equilibrium only: balance clockwise and anticlockwise moments about any chosen point. Translational equilibrium (zero resultant force) and complete equilibrium conditions are deferred to lesson 9702_t04_cm02_l04. Closed vector triangles for coplanar forces are deferred to lesson 9702_t04_cm02_l05.
prior_scope_summaries_consulted: 9702_t04_cm01_l01: Represent distributed weight as acting at the centre of gravity; define and calculate moment of a force using M = F d_perp where d_perp is the perpendicular distance from pivot to line of action.

9702_t04_cm01_l02: Recognise a couple as equal, opposite, parallel forces with separate lines of action; define and calculate torque of a couple as one force multiplied by the perpendicular separation between the forces.

sources_inspected.demands: State the principle of moments. 2 marks awarded for: (1) body in (rotational) equilibrium; (2) sum of clockwise moments about a point equals sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point.

Apply the principle of moments by taking moments about hinge A to determine position x of a 660 N person on a 6.0 m uniform beam of weight 1700 N supported at 5.0 m by a 1300 N upward force from a floating cylinder: (1700 * 3.0) + (660 * x) = (1300 * 5.0) gives x = 2.1 m. Taking moments about hinge A eliminates the unknown hinge reaction force.
State the principle of moments. 2 marks awarded for: (1) in (rotational) equilibrium; (2) sum / total of clockwise moments about a point = sum / total of anticlockwise moments about the (same) point.

Calculate the distance x from central pivot to mass B (45 kg) on a uniform 6.0 m beam balanced horizontally with mass A (60 kg at 3.0 m) and mass C (80 kg at 3.0 m): 80 * 9.81 * 3.0 = (60 * 9.81 * 3.0) + (45 * 9.81 * x) gives x = 1.3 m. Beam weight acts at midpoint directly through pivot, contributing zero moment.

State the principle of moments. 2 marks awarded for: (1) for a body in (rotational) equilibrium; (2) sum/total of clockwise moments about a point = sum/total of anticlockwise moments about the (same) point.

Calculate vertical upward support force FB on a 9.0 m uniform beam of weight 380 N with two pivots B and C (2.0 m from ends) carrying a 750 N person 3.6 m from end D by taking moments about pivot C: (FB * 5.0) = (380 * 2.5) + (750 * 1.6) gives FB = 430 N. Unknown vertical support force FC at pivot C contributes zero moment.

Determine minimum distance x from end D that the person can stand without tipping the beam, recognizing that tipping occurs when contact at pivot B is lost (FB = 0). Taking moments about pivot C: 380 * 2.5 = 750 * (2.0 - x) gives x = 0.7 m.

the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the pivot (point) to the line of action of the force

concepts.name: Prerequisite reminder of single moment calculation and perpendicular distance
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite from lesson 9702_t04_cm01_l01; learners must recall M = F d_perp and recognize that d_perp is the shortest 90-degree distance from the chosen point to the line of action, not simply distance along a sloping member.
misconceptions: Using distance along a sloping beam rather than perpendicular distance to the force line of action.
demands: Recall M = F d_perp and calculate single moments in N m about a chosen reference point.

concepts.name: Prerequisite reminder of couple torque integration
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite from lesson 9702_t04_cm01_l02; a couple has a net torque independent of pivot and can be added directly to the appropriate directional moment sum without multiplying by another distance.
misconceptions: Multiplying the torque of a couple by distance to a pivot, failing to recognize that torque is already a turning effect in N m.
demands: Recall that couple torque is in N m and joins the rotational balance equation directly.

concepts.name: Direction classification of moments about a chosen point
concepts.why_this_depth: Essential procedural skill; students must determine whether each individual force would produce clockwise or anticlockwise rotation about the chosen reference point before summing.
misconceptions: Assuming a downward force is always clockwise regardless of whether it acts to the left or right of the chosen pivot.
Assuming force arrow direction alone determines turning sense without considering pivot position.
demands: Identify whether a force produces clockwise or anticlockwise turning effect about a specified reference point.
Recognize that a downward force on the left turns anticlockwise while a downward force on the right turns clockwise.

concepts.name: The principle of moments and rotational equilibrium
concepts.why_this_depth: Core syllabus outcome 9702_t04_m02_o01 and controlled definition 9702_def_principle_of_moments; mandatory 2-mark recall in Paper 2.
misconceptions: Stating simply that clockwise equals anticlockwise moments while omitting the condition of rotational equilibrium.
Omitting the requirement that both sums must be taken about the same point.
Believing moment balance alone guarantees complete equilibrium (zero resultant force is a separate condition).
demands: State verbatim: for a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point.
Explain that rotational equilibrium means zero angular acceleration / zero net turning effect.

concepts.name: Formulating and solving the rotational balance equation (Sigma M_CW = Sigma M_ACW)
concepts.why_this_depth: Standard multi-mark calculation required in P1 and P2; students must formulate equations with multiple coplanar forces and solve for unknown forces or distances.
misconceptions: Equating clockwise moments about one pivot to anticlockwise moments about a different pivot.
Pairing a force with the wrong distance or summing forces instead of moments.
Neglecting the weight of a uniform beam acting at its midpoint/centre of gravity.
demands: Construct the equation Sigma M_CW = Sigma M_ACW using a single consistent reference point.
Substitute known forces, weights at centres of gravity, and perpendicular distances.
Solve algebraically for an unknown force magnitude or position coordinate x.
Verify dimensional consistency in N m and check numerical balance.

concepts.name: Strategic pivot selection to eliminate unknown forces
concepts.why_this_depth: Decisive problem-solving strategy tested in almost every Cambridge P2 question (e.g. taking moments about a hinge or support pivot to eliminate its unknown reaction force).
misconceptions: Believing that choosing a pivot on a force line makes that force physically vanish from the system, rather than recognizing its moment is zero because d_perp = 0.
Believing moments can only be taken about physical hinges or knife-edges rather than any arbitrary point in the plane.
demands: Recognize that any force whose line of action passes through the chosen reference point has d_perp = 0 and therefore contributes zero moment.
Select a strategic reference point (such as a hinge, pivot, or contact point) that passes through the line of action of an unknown or unneeded reaction force.
Demonstrate that while the force still acts on the body, it drops out of the rotational balance equation.

concepts.name: Zero moment of pivot reaction forces and distinction from force balance
concepts.why_this_depth: Critical conceptual clarity to prepare for lesson cm02_l04; students must understand why reaction forces can be ignored in moment equations but remain real forces required for translational balance.
misconceptions: Assuming pivot reaction forces are always zero in magnitude because their moment is zero.
Confusing zero moment with zero force.
demands: Explain why a pivot reaction force has zero moment about that pivot (d_perp = 0) while having a non-zero moment about other points.
State explicitly that finding an unknown via moments does not mean the system has zero resultant force until translational equilibrium is separately verified.

concepts.name: Tipping condition when a contact reaction force becomes zero
concepts.why_this_depth: Tested in high-demand P2 questions (e.g. 9702_w19_22_q04_b_iii); students must identify the threshold of tipping where a beam loses contact with one pivot.
misconceptions: Believing both supports continue to carry load up to and beyond the tipping threshold.
Failing to set the departing support reaction force to zero in the moment equation.
demands: Identify that when a rigid body is on the verge of tipping about one support, the reaction force at the other support drops to zero.
Take moments about the remaining pivot to solve for critical load positions.

concepts.name: Combined conditions for complete equilibrium (zero resultant force and zero resultant torque)
concepts.why_this_depth: Owned by next lesson 9702_t04_cm02_l04; excluded here to maintain strict pedagogical boundary of rotational balance only.

concepts.name: Closed vector triangles for coplanar forces in equilibrium

hook.historical_investigation: Archimedes' law of the lever and the foundation of static equilibrium (c. 250 BC)
hook.why_this_spine: In his treatise 'On the Equilibrium of Planes', Archimedes established the mathematical foundation of turning effects, demonstrating that unequal weights balance at distances inversely proportional to their weights. This historical investigation provides the ideal narrative spine: it confronts the intuitive misconception that force magnitude alone determines balance and demonstrates how Archimedes used geometric symmetry to prove that turning effect depends strictly on the product of force and distance.

verified_facts.fact: In 'On the Equilibrium of Planes' (Book I, Propositions 6 and 7), Archimedes proved that two magnitudes balance at distances inversely proportional to their weights: w1 * d1 = w2 * d2.
verified_facts.source: Archimedes, 'On the Equilibrium of Planes', c. 250 BC, translated by T. L. Heath, The Works of Archimedes, Cambridge University Press, 1897

verified_facts.fact: Pappus of Alexandria recorded Archimedes' famous assertion of the mechanical advantage of the lever: 'Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth' (Dos moi pou sto, kai kino tan gan).
verified_facts.source: Pappus of Alexandria, 'Synagoge' (Collection), Book VIII, c. 340 AD

verified_facts.fact: Archimedes based his law of the lever on the fundamental postulate that equal weights at equal distances from a fulcrum are in equilibrium.
verified_facts.source: Dijksterhuis, E. J., 'Archimedes', Princeton University Press, 1987, pp. 286-291

hook.closing_question: If a lighter force can overcome a much larger force simply by acting farther from the pivot, what exact physical condition prevents an object from beginning to rotate about any chosen point?

activities.reasoning_step: Classify multiple coplanar forces acting on a pivoted beam as producing clockwise, anticlockwise, or zero turning effects about a designated reference point based on force direction and position relative to the pivot.
misconceptions_addressed: Assuming all downward forces produce clockwise moments regardless of whether they act to the left or right of the pivot.
Failing to identify that a force whose line of action passes directly through the pivot produces zero moment.

activities.reasoning_step: Reconstruct the official Cambridge definition of the principle of moments in precise sequence, ensuring both key conditions (rotational equilibrium and same point) are explicitly included.
misconceptions_addressed: Omitting the essential qualifying condition of rotational equilibrium.
Omitting the requirement that clockwise and anticlockwise moments must be evaluated about the same point.

activities.reasoning_step: Select the optimal pivot point from multiple candidate locations (hinge, center of gravity, cable attachment point, free end) that eliminates an unwanted unknown reaction force from the moment equation in a single step.
misconceptions_addressed: Believing moments can only be taken about physical pivots or fulcrums.
Taking moments about a point that leaves two simultaneous unknown forces in the equation.

activities.reasoning_step: Match given physical beam arrangements (combinations of loads and distances) to their correct algebraic rotational balance equations (Sigma M_CW = Sigma M_ACW).
misconceptions_addressed: Pairing a force with another force distance rather than its own distance from the pivot.
Adding clockwise and anticlockwise moments on the same side of the equation without sign distinction.

activities.reasoning_step: Evaluate the physical condition when a beam supported on two pivots is about to tip as a load shifts outward, identifying which pivot reaction force vanishes and setting up the moment balance about the remaining pivot.
misconceptions_addressed: Assuming both supports share the load equally even when the beam begins to lift off one support.
Believing the reaction force at the tipping fulcrum becomes zero instead of the reaction force at the far support.
